The PDM stays as published. What can still be improved is everything around it: what the
calibration counts as a good fit, which parameters it bothers to fit, how a model is judged,
whether it holds when conditions change, and how sure we are of it. Six articles take these in
turn, each on the same made-up catchment, so that every answer can be checked against the truth.

| Question | Article | Functions |
|---|---|---|
| Does the calibration count every error fairly? | [Counting every error fairly](fair-errors.html) | `objective = "boxcox"`, `boxcox_flow()`, `flow_weights()` |
| Which parameters can the record determine? | [Global sensitivity](global-sensitivity.html) | `pdm_sensitivity()` |
| Which model forecasts best? | [Choosing a model as a forecaster](forecast-choice.html) | `compare_forecasts()` |
| Will the calibration hold in other years? | [Stress tests](stress-tests.html) | `split_sample_test()`, `parameter_drift()` |
| How sure are we of the parameters and the forecast? | [Bayesian calibration](bayesian-calibration.html) | `calibrate_bayes()`, `posterior_band()`, priors |
| Is a probability forecast honest? | [Ensemble verification](ensemble-verification.html) | `ensemble_scores()`, `crps_ensemble()`, `brier_score()` |

# How they fit together

**Before calibrating**, a global sensitivity analysis on the structure's full bounds shows which
parameters the record can determine. Fix the rest at a regional or default value: fewer free
parameters, fewer equally good answers, calibrations that agree.

**Calibrating**, the Box-Cox objective counts every hour's error alike instead of letting a few
floods decide, and rating weights let flows the gauge measures poorly count for less. Choose the
power so the errors are the same size at every flow; the first article shows how.

**Choosing between candidates**, judge them as forecasters: hindcast skill at the lead times the
service uses, and threshold warnings, not the score of a simulation of the whole record.

**Checking the choice**, calibrate on dry years and score wet ones, and calibrate period by
period to catch a change in the catchment or the record that a single calibration would hide.

**Quantifying the uncertainty**, a Bayesian calibration samples every set consistent with the
record and the priors; with priors from a model of parameters from catchment descriptors, it
also serves catchments with short records, or none. Its predictive band, and any ensemble
forecast built on it, should then be checked for honesty with the ensemble scores.

# What these do not cover

They treat the rainfall as given. Parameters absorb the habits of the rainfall they were fitted
on, so the largest single improvement is to calibrate on the same catchment rainfall product,
built the same way, that is used to forecast ([Catchment rainfall from gauges and
radar](rainfall.html)).
